title: Bird Arrival at a Nesting Area
topic: Rate Models, Riemann Sums, and the IVT

stimulus.content:
Male birds of a certain species arrive at a nesting area over a thirty-day period. The rate at which the male birds arrive at the nesting area at time t days is modeled by a differentiable function M, where M(t) is measured in number of birds per day. Selected values of M(t) are shown in the table.

t (days): 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30
M(t) (birds per day): 2, 7, 16, 6, 5, 2, 0

Note: the calculator should be in radian mode.

prompt: Male birds of a certain species arrive at a nesting area over a thirty-day period. The rate at which the male birds arrive at the nesting area at time t days is modeled by a differentiable function M, where M(t) is measured in number of birds per day. Selected values of M(t) are shown in the table.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Approximate \( M'(7.5) \) using the average rate of change of M over the interval \( 5 \le t \le 10 \). Show the work that leads to your answer, and indicate units of measure.

rubricPoints.criterion: Computes the average rate of change \( M'(7.5) \approx (M(10) - M(5))/(10 - 5) = (16 - 7)/5 = 9/5 = 1.8 \), with supporting work showing both a difference and a quotient.
commonErrors: uses endpoints [0, 10] or [7.5, 10] instead of [5, 10]
gives only the numerical value 9/5 with no difference and quotient
computes M(10) - M(5) = 9 with no quotient
uses (16 - 7)/(15 - 0) or another incorrect denominator
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Writes only "9/5" with no supporting work, or uses the wrong interval

rubricPoints.criterion: Reports correct units: "birds per day per day" (equivalently \( birds/day^2 \)).
commonErrors: states units as "birds"
states units as "birds per day" without the second per-day
gives no units at all
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Appends "birds per day per day" to the computed value
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Reports 1.8 with no units or with units of "birds per day"

parts.label: (b) i.
parts.text: Use a midpoint Riemann sum with the three subintervals [0, 10], [10, 20], and [20, 30] to approximate \( \int_0^{30} M(t)\,dt \). Show the work that leads to your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: Presents the form of a midpoint Riemann sum: \( 7(10) + 6(10) + 2(10) \), i.e. \( M(5)(10-0) + M(15)(20-10) + M(25)(30-20) \), with at least five of the six factors correct.
commonErrors: uses left or right endpoints instead of midpoints
has more than one incorrect factor (wrong function value or width)
writes a single term like M(15).30 as the whole sum
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Writes 16(10) + 6(10) + 2(10) with the first function value taken from the wrong column

rubricPoints.criterion: Evaluates the sum to 150 with supporting work \( (70 + 60 + 20) \).
commonErrors: arithmetic error while summing 70, 60, and 20
reports "150" with no supporting work (unsupported answer)
evaluates a left/right sum instead of the midpoint sum
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Writes 150 by itself with no form of the sum shown

parts.label: (b) ii.
parts.text: Interpret the meaning of \( \int_0^{30} M(t)\,dt \) in the context of the problem.

rubricPoints.criterion: States that the integral represents the number of male birds of this species that arrive at the nesting area from \( t = 0 \) days to \( t = 30 \) days.
commonErrors: says the integral is a rate of arrival
describes an average rate instead of a total
omits the time interval t = 0 to t = 30
does not mention that birds arrived
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Says it is the total number of male birds that arrive over the 30 days
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Says "the rate at which birds arrive" or leaves out the interval

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: The rate at which female birds of the same species arrive at the same nesting area, in birds per day, is modeled by the function F defined as follows: \( F(t) = 0 \) for \( 0 \le t < 15 \); \( F(t) = 18 + 16\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{20}(t+15)\right) \) for \( 15 \le t \le 45 \). How many female birds of this species arrive at the nesting area from \( t = 15 \) to \( t = 45 \)? Show the setup for your calculations, and round your answer to the nearest integer.

rubricPoints.criterion: Sets up the definite integral \( \int_{15}^{45} F(t)\,dt \) (with or without the differential dt).
commonErrors: uses limits 0 to 30 or 15 to 30
writes \int_{15}^{45} M(t)\,dt using the wrong function
omits the integral and jumps to the numeric answer

rubricPoints.criterion: Evaluates the integral to 641.859 and rounds to 642 birds.
commonErrors: computes in degree mode and gets a wildly different value
reports 641 without rounding up
arithmetic error in the antiderivative 18t - \frac{320}{\pi}\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{20}(t+15)\right)
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Evaluates to 641.859164 and reports 642 birds to the nearest integer
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Reports 641.859 as the final answer without rounding to an integer

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: On the interval \( 15 < t < 30 \), the difference in the rates at which male and female birds of this species arrive at the nesting area can be modeled by the differentiable function \( D(t) = M(t) - F(t) \), where F is the function defined in part (c). Is there a time \( t \) in the interval \( 15 < t < 20 \) when \( D(t) = 0 \)? Justify your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: States that D is continuous because D is differentiable (or equivalent).
commonErrors: states "D is continuous" with no justification
says M or F is continuous without connecting to differentiability
attempts IVT without mentioning continuity at all
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Writes "Because D is differentiable, D is continuous."
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Writes only "D is continuous" with no reason

rubricPoints.criterion: Applies the Intermediate Value Theorem: \( D(15) = 4 > 0 \) and \( D(20) = -1.686292 < 0 \), so there is a \( t \) in \( (15, 20) \) with \( D(t) = 0 \).
commonErrors: computes D(15) or D(20) incorrectly
gives both endpoint values but no conclusion
writes "yes, IVT" without citing D(15) > 0 and D(20) < 0
names the wrong theorem
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Shows D(15) = 4 > 0, D(20) = -1.686292 < 0, concludes by IVT that D(t) = 0 for some t in (15, 20)
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Answers "yes" based only on the sign change with no continuity statement and no endpoint values

sampleResponse: (a) \( M'(7.5) \approx \frac{M(10)-M(5)}{10-5} = \frac{16-7}{5} = \frac{9}{5} = 1.8 \) birds per day per day. (b) i. \( \int_0^{30} M(t)\,dt \approx M(5)(10-0) + M(15)(20-10) + M(25)(30-20) = 7(10) + 6(10) + 2(10) = 150 \). ii. The integral gives the total number of male birds that arrive at the nesting area from \( t = 0 \) to \( t = 30 \) days. (c) \( \int_{15}^{45} F(t)\,dt = \int_{15}^{45}\left(18 + 16\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{20}(t+15)\right)\right)\,dt = 641.859164 \), so to the nearest integer the number of female birds is 642. (d) Since D is differentiable, D is continuous; \( D(15) = M(15) - F(15) = 6 - 2 = 4 > 0 \) and \( D(20) = M(20) - F(20) = 5 - 6.686292 = -1.686292 < 0 \), so by the Intermediate Value Theorem there is a time \( t \) with \( 15 < t < 20 \) and \( D(t) = 0 \).

title: Area and Volume of Two Functions

stimulus.content: Figure 1 shows the graphs of f and g in the first quadrant, intersecting at the points (1, 2) and (a, b), with region R under g from x = 0 to x = 1 and a shaded region between f and g from x = 0 to x = a. Figure 2 shows the graph of x = h(y) and the horizontal line y = 3.5. (Examination figures are not embedded in this data file.)

prompt: The function f is defined by \( f(x) = 1.43^x + 0.57 \), and the function g is defined by \( g(x) = \frac{14x+12}{x+12} \). The graphs of f and g intersect at the points (1, 2) and (a, b), as shown in Figure 1. For \( x \ge 0 \), the equation \( y = g(x) \) can be rewritten as \( x = \frac{12y-12}{14-y} = h(y) \), where h is a function of y. The graph of \( x = h(y) \) and the horizontal line \( y = 3.5 \) are shown in Figure 2.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Let R be the region bounded by the graph of g, the x-axis, the y-axis, and the vertical line \( x = 1 \), as shown in Figure 1. Find the area of region R. Show the setup for your calculations.

rubricPoints.criterion: Sets up the area of R as \( \int_0^1 g(x)\,dx \) (or \( \int_0^1 \frac{14x+12}{x+12}\,dx \)), with or without the differential dx.
commonErrors: writes \int_0^1 (f(x) - g(x))\,dx or \int_0^a g(x)\,dx
writes \int_1^2 g(x)\,dx with wrong limits
forgets the differential dx
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Writes \int g(x)\,dx with no limits or \int_0^1 f(x)\,dx

rubricPoints.criterion: Evaluates the integral to 1.513338 and reports the area as 1.513.
commonErrors: uses the wrong antiderivative form (the correct antiderivative is 14x - 156\ln(x+12))
reports 1.5133 with a rounding error
writes the value with an inappropriate number of decimal places
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Evaluates correctly but reports 1.474 (mixing up sign of the log term)

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Region R, described in part (a), is the base of a solid. For this solid, each cross section perpendicular to the x-axis is a rectangle whose height is \( \frac{1}{3} \) times the length of its base in region R. Write, but do not evaluate, an integral expression that gives the volume of the solid.

rubricPoints.criterion: Presents an integrand of the form \( k(g(x))^2 \) in a definite or indefinite integral, where k is any nonzero constant (e.g. \( \frac{1}{3}(g(x))^2 \)).
commonErrors: writes \frac{1}{3}(g(x))^2 outside an integral
uses k(g(x))^3 or k\cdot g(x) instead of k(g(x))^2
uses the base length raised to a power other than 2

rubricPoints.criterion: Writes the correct definite integral \( \frac{1}{3}\int_0^1 (g(x))^2\,dx \) (with or without the differential dx).
commonErrors: uses limits other than 0 to 1
omits the leading constant \frac{1}{3}
leaves the integral indefinite
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Writes Volume = \int_0^1 (g(x))^2\,dx with no constant of \frac{1}{3}

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: The shaded region in Figure 1 is bounded by the graphs of f and g on the interval from \( x = 0 \) to \( x = a \). Find the area of the shaded region. Show the setup for your calculations.

rubricPoints.criterion: Presents an integrand of \( f(x) - g(x) \) (or \( g(x) - f(x) \)) in a definite integral, with or without the differential dx.
commonErrors: writes |f(x) - g(x)| outside an integral
uses f(x) + g(x) as the integrand
gives only a numeric answer with no integrand
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Writes \int_0^a |f(x) - g(x)| outside an integral with no setup

rubricPoints.criterion: Writes the correct definite integral with limits \( x = 0 \) to \( x = a \) (a reported value must be 3, 3.2, 3.3, 3.25, 3.26, 3.255, or 3.256 to be eligible), or an equivalent sum such as \( \int_0^1 (f(x)-g(x))\,dx + \int_1^a (g(x)-f(x))\,dx \).
commonErrors: uses a value of a other than the accepted rounded values
integrates 0 to a with f - g but never resolves the sign (f is above g on (0,1))
uses limits 0 to 1 instead of 0 to a
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Writes \int_0^{3.255817} (f(x) - g(x))\,dx or the split sum \int_0^1 (f-g)\,dx + \int_1^a (g-f)\,dx
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Writes \int_0^a (f(x) - g(x))\,dx with a reported as 2 or 4

rubricPoints.criterion: Evaluates the integral to 0.631784 and reports the area as 0.632 (or 0.631).
commonErrors: evaluates \int_0^a (f - g)\,dx without the sign split and gets a negative value
reports 0.63 or 0.6317 with incorrect rounding to three places
arithmetic error in the antiderivative of 1.43^x (which is 1.43^x / \ln 1.43)
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Computes the area as 0.631784 and reports 0.632
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Reports 0.63 or a negative area without re-expressing the split integral

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Let T be the region bounded by the graph of \( x = h(y) \), the y-axis, and the horizontal line \( y = 3.5 \), as shown in Figure 2. Write, but do not evaluate, an integral expression that gives the volume of the solid generated when region T is revolved about the y-axis.

rubricPoints.criterion: Presents an integrand of the form \( k(h(y))^2 \) in a definite or indefinite integral, where k is any nonzero constant (e.g. \( \pi(h(y))^2 \) or \( \pi\left(\frac{12y-12}{14-y}\right)^2 \)).
commonErrors: uses the integrand \pi(h(y)) without squaring
integrates with respect to x instead of y
uses the shell method form without the correct radius

rubricPoints.criterion: Writes the correct definite integral \( \pi\int_1^{3.5} (h(y))^2\,dy \), including the constant \( \pi \), limits \( y = 1 \) to \( y = 3.5 \), and the differential dy.
commonErrors: uses limits 0 to 3.5 or 0 to 2
omits the factor \pi
integrates from y = 1 to y = 3.5 in the wrong order
omits dy

sampleResponse: (a) Area = \( \int_0^1 g(x)\,dx = \int_0^1 \frac{14x+12}{x+12}\,dx = [14x - 156\ln(x+12)]_0^1 = 1.513338 \), so the area of R is 1.513. (b) Volume = \( \frac{1}{3}\int_0^1 (g(x))^2\,dx \). (c) At the intersections \( f(x) = g(x) \) gives \( x = 1 \) and \( x = 3.255817 = a \). The area is \( \int_0^1 (f(x)-g(x))\,dx + \int_1^a (g(x)-f(x))\,dx = 0.631784 \), so the area of the shaded region is 0.632. (d) Volume = \( \pi\int_1^{3.5} (h(y))^2\,dy \).

title: Pie Cooling

stimulus.content: The examination shows a slope field of line segments (all of which have positive slopes in the printed figure) beside the differential equation. (Examination figure not embedded in this data file.)

prompt: A pie is taken from a hot oven and put on a table. The internal temperature of the pie at time \( t \) minutes can be modeled by the function H that satisfies the differential equation \( \frac{dH}{dt} = -\frac{1}{15}(H - 20) \), where \( H(t) \) is measured in degrees Celsius and \( H(0) = 75 \). For \( t > 0 \), it is known that \( 20 < H(t) < 75 \).

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Explain why the slope field shown could not be a slope field for the differential equation \( \frac{dH}{dt} = -\frac{1}{15}(H - 20) \).

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains that every segment in the shown slope field has a positive slope, while the differential equation gives \( \frac{dH}{dt} < 0 \) on \( 20 < H < 75 \) (so all true slopes are negative).
commonErrors: refers only to the sign of dH/dt without connecting it to the slope field
says "there are no negative slopes shown" but never ties it to dH/dt < 0
refers to the slope of the differential equation or the "increasing behavior" of the slope field
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Writes that all slopes in the field are positive but the differential equation requires negative slopes since H - 20 > 0
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Writes "the slopes should be negative" with no reference to the slope field given

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Find the slope of the line tangent to the graph of H at time \( t = 0 \). Show the work that leads to your answer.

commonErrors: uses H - 20 with the wrong value of H
sign error producing +11/3
simplifies -55/15 to something other than -11/3

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: It can be shown that \( \frac{d^2H}{dt^2} = \frac{1}{225}(H - 20) \). The line tangent to the graph of H at time \( t = 0 \) is used to approximate \( H(5) \), the internal temperature of the pie at time \( t = 5 \). Is this approximation an overestimate or an underestimate for the actual value of \( H(5) \)? Give a reason for your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: Considers the sign of \( \frac{d^2H}{dt^2} \) (symbolically or in words): since \( 20 < H < 75 \) for \( t > 0 \), \( \frac{d^2H}{dt^2} > 0 \).
commonErrors: does not establish the sign of the second derivative
states \frac{d^2H}{dt^2} < 0
references the concavity of the tangent line instead of H
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Concludes the concavity without considering the sign of \frac{d^2H}{dt^2}

rubricPoints.criterion: Concludes the approximation is an underestimate because the graph of H is concave up so the tangent line lies below the graph.
commonErrors: says "concave up, so overestimate"
gives the concavity but no conclusion
bases the answer on dH/dt being negative instead of concavity
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: States that since H is concave up the tangent line lies below the graph, so the approximation underestimates H(5)

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Use separation of variables to find an expression for \( H(t) \), the particular solution to the given differential equation with initial condition \( H(0) = 75 \).

rubricPoints.criterion: Separates the variables into an equation of the form \( \frac{dH}{H-20} = -\frac{1}{15}\,dt \) (constants nonzero).
commonErrors: no separation of variables in the work
separates as \frac{dH}{H+20}
sign error in the dt side
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Integrates the differential equation without separating variables

rubricPoints.criterion: Finds one consistent antiderivative of the form \( \ln|H - 20| \) or \( -\frac{t}{15} \) (with or without absolute value).
commonErrors: writes \ln(H+20) instead of \ln(H-20)
writes \frac{t}{15} with the wrong sign
forgets the chain-rule factor of 1/15

rubricPoints.criterion: Finds two consistent antiderivatives ( \( \ln|H-20| \) and the t-side antiderivative).
commonErrors: gives only one side of the antiderivative
antiderivatives inconsistent with the separated equation

rubricPoints.criterion: Includes the constant of integration and uses the initial condition: \( \ln(75-20) = 0 + C \), so \( C = \ln 55 \).
commonErrors: no constant of integration anywhere
substitutes H = 75 at t = 0 into the solution instead of the antiderivative step
wrong C value
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Substitutes t = 0, H = 75 to find C = \ln 55
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Omits C entirely and never applies the initial condition

rubricPoints.criterion: Solves for \( H(t) \) correctly: \( H(t) = 20 + 55e^{-t/15} \) (or equivalent).
commonErrors: exponentiates to H - 20 = 55e^{+t/15}
writes H(t) = 75e^{-t/15} + 20 with the wrong coefficient
drops the +20

sampleResponse: (a) For the slope field shown all segment slopes are positive, but \( \frac{dH}{dt} = -\frac{1}{15}(H-20) < 0 \) for \( 20 < H < 75 \), so the shown field cannot be a slope field for this equation. (b) \( \frac{dH}{dt}\bigg|_{(0,75)} = -\frac{1}{15}(75-20) = -\frac{55}{15} = -\frac{11}{3} \). (c) Since \( 20 < H < 75 \), \( \frac{d^2H}{dt^2} = \frac{H-20}{225} > 0 \), so H is concave up and the tangent line lies below the graph; therefore the approximation is an underestimate for \( H(5) \). (d) Separating variables: \( \frac{dH}{H-20} = -\frac{1}{15}\,dt \), so \( \ln|H-20| = -\frac{t}{15} + C \). Using \( H(0) = 75 \) gives \( C = \ln 55 \), hence \( H(t) = 20 + 55e^{-t/15} \).

title: Graph of f prime

stimulus.content: The examination includes the graph of f' on the closed interval [-4, 4]. In that graph: f'(x) = 0 at x = -2 and x = 3; f'(x) < 0 for -4 < x < -2; f'(x) > 0 for -2 < x < 3 and for 3 < x < 4; and f' changes from increasing to decreasing at x = 1. (Examination figure not embedded in this data file.)

prompt: Let f be a twice-differentiable function on the closed interval \( [-4, 4] \) with \( f(2) = 3 \). The graph of \( f' \), the derivative of f, is shown.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: For \( x > 0 \), the function g is defined by \( g(x) = f(x) - \ln x \). Find \( g'(2) \). Show the work that leads to your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: Sets up the derivative \( g'(x) = f'(x) - \frac{1}{x} \) (or evaluates \( g'(2) = f'(2) - \frac{1}{2} \)).
commonErrors: writes g'(x) = f'(x) + \frac{1}{x} with the wrong sign on the log term
differentiates the logarithm incorrectly (1/x correct, forgetting it entirely is wrong)
omits the setup and jumps to the answer
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Writes g'(x) = f'(x) - \ln(x) (never differentiates the log term)

commonErrors: reads f'(2) as 3/2 incorrectly
arithmetic error computing 1.5 - 0.5
unsupported answer of 1 (earns P2 but not P1)

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Find all values of x on the open interval \( 0 < x < 3 \) at which the graph of f has a point of inflection. Give a reason for your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: Answers \( x = 1 \) (with no other values declared in \( 0 < x < 3 \)).
commonErrors: also declares other values in 0 < x < 3 as inflection points
gives a point (1, a) instead of the x-value (earns the value but not the reason point)
answers x = 3 or x = -3 in addition
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Writes "The graph of f has a point of inflection at x = 1"
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Lists x = 1 and x = 2 as inflection points

rubricPoints.criterion: Gives a reason tied to the graph of \( f' \): \( f' \) changes from increasing to decreasing (or \( f' \) attains a relative maximum / the slope of \( f' \) changes sign) at \( x = 1 \).
commonErrors: says "f changes concavity there" without reference to f'
says "f'' changes sign there" (does not reference the given graph of f')
uses an ambiguous phrase like "the function" or "the graph"
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Writes that f' changes from increasing to decreasing at x = 1
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Writes "x = 1 because f changes concavity" with no link to f'

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: For \( -4 \le x \le 4 \), on what open intervals, if any, is the graph of f both increasing and concave down? Give a reason for your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: Answers \( 1 < x < 3 \) (this interval, with or without endpoints included).
commonErrors: gives -2 < x < 3 (increasing only)
gives 1 < x < 3 but includes extra intervals
writes "if any" and says none
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Writes "f is increasing and concave down on 1 < x < 3"

rubricPoints.criterion: Gives a reason that refers to \( f' \) and cites both \( f'(x) > 0 \) and \( f' \) decreasing on the interval.
commonErrors: cites only f'(x) > 0
cites only that f' is decreasing
never refers to f'
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Writes "f'(x) > 0 and f' is decreasing on 1 < x < 3"
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Writes only "f is increasing there because f'(x) > 0"

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: For \( -4 \le x \le 4 \), find the value of x at which f has an absolute minimum and the value of x at which f has an absolute maximum. Give reasons for your answers.

rubricPoints.criterion: Considers \( f'(x) = 0 \) (e.g. by examining the graph or saying "critical points"), regardless of whether both roots are found.
commonErrors: does not consider where f' = 0 at all
presents x = -2 and x = 3 with no mention of f' = 0 or critical points
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Lists "x = -2 and x = 3" with no reference to f' = 0

rubricPoints.criterion: Declares the absolute minimum at \( x = -2 \) with a correct justification (\( f' \) changes from negative to positive, or a sign analysis of \( f' \)).
commonErrors: declares the minimum without justification
argues the minimum is at x = 4
correct answer but reason not tied to the graph of f'
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Notes f'(x) < 0 for -4 < x < -2 and f'(x) > 0 for -2 < x < 3, so f attains an absolute minimum at x = -2
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Writes "minimum at x = -2" with no reason

rubricPoints.criterion: Declares the absolute maximum at \( x = 4 \) with a correct justification (\( f(4) > f(-4) \), since the net area under \( f' \) above the x-axis from \( -4 \) to \( 4 \) is positive).
commonErrors: declares the maximum at x = 4 with no endpoint comparison
claims the maximum is at x = 3 (a flat spot of f', not an extremum)
fails to compare the endpoints f(4) and f(-4)
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Notes f decreases to x = -2 then increases, and compares endpoints: \int_{-4}^4 f'(x)\,dx = f(4) - f(-4) > 0, so the maximum is at x = 4
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Answers "maximum at x = 4" citing only that f'(x) > 0 there

sampleResponse: (a) \( g'(x) = f'(x) - \frac{1}{x} \), so \( g'(2) = f'(2) - \frac{1}{2} = \frac{3}{2} - \frac{1}{2} = 1 \). (b) The graph of f has a point of inflection at \( x = 1 \) because \( f' \) changes from increasing to decreasing there. (c) f is increasing and concave down on \( 1 < x < 3 \) because \( f'(x) > 0 \) and \( f' \) is decreasing on that interval. (d) \( f'(x) = 0 \) at \( x = -2 \) and \( x = 3 \). Since \( f' < 0 \) to the left of \( -2 \) and \( f' > 0 \) to the right, f has an absolute minimum at \( x = -2 \). On \( [-4, 4] \), f increases after \( x = -2 \), and \( f(4) - f(-4) = \int_{-4}^4 f'(x)\,dx > 0 \) (area above the axis exceeds area below), so f has an absolute maximum at \( x = 4 \).

title: Toy Car Motion

stimulus.content: The examination includes the graph of v(t) on [0, 12]. (Examination figure not embedded in this data file.)

prompt: A remote-controlled toy car moves back and forth along a straight path so that its velocity at time t is given by the function v, where \( v(t) \) is measured in feet per second and \( t \) is measured in seconds. \( v(t) = t^4 - 8t^3 + 16t^2 \) for \( 0 \le t \le 4 \); \( v(t) = 0 \) for \( 4 < t < 6 \); \( v(t) = 10\cos\left(\frac{\pi t}{3}\right) - 10 \) for \( 6 \le t \le 12 \). The graph of \( v(t) \) is shown.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Find the acceleration of the car at time \( t = 1 \) second. Show the work that leads to your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: Considers \( v'(t) \): \( a(t) = v'(t) = 4t^3 - 24t^2 + 32t \) (or considers \( v'(1) \) directly).
commonErrors: writes a(t) = 4t^3 + 24t^2 + 32t with a sign error
copies the quartic coefficient into the derivative incorrectly

rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Writes a(1) = 12 with no derivative shown

arithmetic error in 4 - 24 + 32
unsupported answer of 12

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Find the distance, in feet, that the car traveled over the time interval \( 0 \le t \le 4 \) seconds. Show the work that leads to your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: Sets up the definite integral \( \int_0^4 v(t)\,dt \) (or \( \int_0^4 (t^4 - 8t^3 + 16t^2)\,dt \)), with or without dt.
commonErrors: integrates over 0 to 12 instead of 0 to 4
uses |v(t)| when the velocity does not change sign (acceptable but unnecessary)

rubricPoints.criterion: Finds the correct antiderivative \( \frac{t^5}{5} - 2t^4 + \frac{16t^3}{3} \).
commonErrors: writes \frac{t^5}{4} instead of \frac{t^5}{5}
sign errors in the -2t^4 term
wrong constant on \frac{16t^3}{3}

rubricPoints.criterion: Evaluates the definite integral to \( \frac{512}{15} \) feet.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Find the average velocity of the car over the time interval \( 6 \le t \le 12 \) seconds. Show the work that leads to your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: Sets up the average value formula \( \frac{1}{12-6}\int_6^{12} v(t)\,dt \) (or \( \frac{1}{6}\int_6^{12} (10\cos(\pi t/3) - 10)\,dt \)), with evidence of division by 6.
commonErrors: forgets the factor 1/6
integrates 0 to 12
uses the average of the endpoint velocities only

rubricPoints.criterion: Finds an antiderivative of the form \( 10\cdot\frac{3}{\pi}\sin\left(\frac{\pi t}{3}\right) - 10t \) (including the \( 1/6 \) factor where combined).

forgets the -10t term
wrong constant in the sin antiderivative
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Writes an antiderivative whose sin coefficient is not 30/\pi

rubricPoints.criterion: Evaluates the average velocity as -10 feet per second.

forgets to divide by 6 at the end

sampleResponse: (a) \( a(t) = v'(t) = 4t^3 - 24t^2 + 32t \), so \( a(1) = 4 - 24 + 32 = 12 \) \( ft/s^2 \). (b) \( v(1) = 1 - 8 + 16 = 9 > 0 \) and \( v'(1) = 12 > 0 \); since velocity and acceleration have the same sign, the car is speeding up at \( t = 1 \). (c) Distance = \( \int_0^4 (t^4 - 8t^3 + 16t^2)\,dt = \left[\frac{t^5}{5} - 2t^4 + \frac{16t^3}{3}\right]_0^4 = \frac{512}{15} \) feet. title: Table of Values of f and f prime

The function f is twice differentiable. The table gives values of f and its derivative f' at selected values of x.

title: Invasive Species Spread
topic: Average Value, Mean Value Theorem, Limits, and Optimization

stimulus.content: The question presents no figure. The calculator should be in radian mode.

prompt: An invasive species of plant appears in a fruit grove at time \( t = 0 \) and begins to spread. The function C defined by \( C(t) = 7.6\arctan(0.2t) \) models the number of acres in the fruit grove affected by the species t weeks after the species appears. It can be shown that \( C'(t) = \frac{38}{25 + t^2} \). (Note: Your calculator should be in radian mode.)

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Find the average number of acres affected by the invasive species from time \( t = 0 \) to time \( t = 4 \) weeks. Show the setup for your calculations.

rubricPoints.criterion: Presents the average value formula \( \frac{1}{4 - 0}\int_0^4 C(t)\,dt = \frac{1}{4}\int_0^4 C(t)\,dt \), i.e. a correct integral together with evidence of division by 4 (with or without the differential dt).
commonErrors: presents only \( \int_0^4 C(t)\,dt \) with no factor of \( \frac{1}{4} \)
uses the average rate of change \( \frac{C(4)-C(0)}{4-0} \) instead of the average value
omits the differential dt and treats the whole expression as the antiderivative
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: \frac{1}{4}\int_0^4 C(t)\,dt = \frac{1}{4}\int_0^4 7.6\arctan(0.2t)\,dt or the integral together with the correct answer 2.778224
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: \int_0^4 C(t)\,dt = 11.112896 with no division by 4 and no average value

rubricPoints.criterion: Gives the correct answer 2.778 (or 2.778224), with or without supporting work, accurate to three places after the decimal point.
commonErrors: reports 11.112896, the value of the integral before dividing by 4
reports the answer to only two decimal places
reports the average rate of change 1.282 instead of the average value

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Find the time \( t \) when the instantaneous rate of change of C equals the average rate of change of C over the time interval \( 0 \le t \le 4 \). Show the setup for your calculations.

rubricPoints.criterion: Presents the average rate of change \( \frac{C(4)-C(0)}{4-0} \) and evaluates it to 1.282008, or an equivalent expression such as \( \frac{1}{4}\int_0^4 C'(t)\,dt \).
commonErrors: presents only t = 1.282 (the value of the average rate of change itself) as the answer
computes \( \frac{C(4)-C(0)}{2} \) with the wrong denominator
presents the average rate of change expression but never evaluates it
solves \( C'(t) = 0 \) instead of \( C'(t) = 1.282008 \)
reports 1.282 (the rate value) instead of the time
solves \( C(t) = 1.282008 \), finding a time where the number of acres, not the rate, equals the average rate

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Assume that the invasive species continues to spread according to the given model for all times \( t > 0 \). Write a limit expression that describes the end behavior of the rate of change in the number of acres affected by the species. Evaluate this limit expression.

rubricPoints.criterion: Writes a limit expression for the end behavior of the rate of change: \( \lim_{t \to \infty} C'(t) = \lim_{t \to \infty}\frac{38}{25 + t^2} \) (or \( \lim_{t \to \infty} C(t) \)).
commonErrors: usesthe limit as t approaches 0 instead of t approaching infinity
writes no limit notation and just gives the rational expression
writes \( \lim_{x \to \infty} \) with the wrong variable

rubricPoints.criterion: Evaluates the limit to 0. (A response whose limit expression is \( \lim_{t\to\infty} C(t) \), not \( \lim_{t\to\infty} C'(t) \), is not eligible; arithmetic with infinity such as substituting \( \infty \) is treated as scratch work.)
commonErrors: writes \( \frac{38}{25 + \infty^2} = 0 \), i.e. arithmetic with infinity
evaluates \( \lim_{t \to \infty} C(t) = \frac{76}{5}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2} \) and reports that as the rate's limiting value
reports a nonzero value

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: At time \( t = 4 \) weeks after the invasive species appears in the fruit grove, measures are taken to counter the spread of the species. The function A, defined by \( A(t) = C(t) - 0.1\int_4^t \ln(x)\,dx \), models the number of acres affected by the species over the time interval \( 4 \le t \le 36 \). At what time \( t \), for \( 4 \le t \le 36 \), does A attain its maximum value? Justify your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: Considers \( A'(t) = 0 \), \( C'(t) - 0.1\ln t = 0 \), or \( C'(t) = 0.1\ln t \) (or discusses the sign of \( A'(t) \) changing or the critical points of A).
commonErrors: just presents t = 11.441700 with no equation
differentiates A incorrectly (forgets the fundamental theorem term \( 0.1\ln t \) )
solves \( C'(t) = 0 \) alone

rubricPoints.criterion: Makes a global argument: evaluates and compares \( A(4) = 5.128 \), \( A(11.441700) = 7.317 \), and \( A(36) = 1.743 \) (candidates test), or shows \( A'(t) > 0 \) for \( 4 < t < 11.442 \) and \( A'(t) < 0 \) for \( 11.442 < t < 36 \).
commonErrors: gives only a local argument (First or Second Derivative Test) with no global comparison
omits one of the three candidate evaluations (4, 11.441700, 36)
evaluates A incorrectly at one of the candidates
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: sign change of A' alone with no global comparison

rubricPoints.criterion: Reports the time \( t = 11.442 \) (or 11.441), with supporting work.
commonErrors: reports the maximum value 7.317 instead of the time
reports t = 36 or t = 4
gives 11.442 with no work
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Therefore the number of acres is maximum at t = 11.442 weeks

sampleResponse: (a) The average number of acres is \( \frac{1}{4}\int_0^4 C(t)\,dt = \frac{1}{4}(11.112896) = 2.778224 \), so 2.778 acres. (b) The average rate of change over \( 0 \le t \le 4 \) is \( \frac{C(4)-C(0)}{4-0} = 1.282008 \). Setting \( C'(t) = 1.282008 \) gives \( t = 2.154298 \), so the time is 2.154. (c) \( \lim_{t \to \infty} C'(t) = \lim_{t \to \infty}\frac{38}{25 + t^2} = 0 \). (d) \( A'(t) = C'(t) - 0.1\ln t \), so \( A'(t) = 0 \) gives \( \frac{38}{25 + t^2} = 0.1\ln t \) and \( t = 11.441700 \). Comparing \( A(4) = 5.128031 \), \( A(11.441700) = 7.316978 \), and \( A(36) = 1.743056 \), the maximum occurs at \( t = 11.442 \).

title: Area, Volume, and Washers

stimulus.content: The figure shows the graphs of f and g on [0, 3], with f below g, bounding the shaded region R. (The figure image is shown to the student.)

prompt: The shaded region R is bounded by the graphs of the functions f and g, where \( f(x) = x^2 - 2x \) and \( g(x) = x + \sin(\pi x) \), as shown in the figure. (Note: Your calculator should be in radian mode.) (The graph of f and g in the figure is not embedded in this data file.)

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Find the area of R. Show the setup for your calculations.

rubricPoints.criterion: Presents an integrand of \( g(x) - f(x) \) (or \( f(x) - g(x) \)) in a definite integral with the limits 0 to 3, with or without the differential dx.
commonErrors: uses the integrand \( g(x) \) or \( f(x) \) alone (missing the difference)
writes \( 2x - x^2 \) (a sign error in the difference) in the integral
omits the limits of integration
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: \int_0^3 g(x)\,dx alone or a difference of the wrong sign with no resolution

rubricPoints.criterion: Evaluates to 5.136620 and reports the area as 5.137 (or 5.136), accurate to three places after the decimal point.
commonErrors: reports -5.137 while claiming the area is positive (using f - g without resolving the sign)
reports 4.5 (forgetting the \( \sin \) integral term)
reports the answer with too few decimal places

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Region R is the base of a solid. For this solid, at each x the cross section perpendicular to the x-axis is a rectangle with height x and base in region R. Find the volume of the solid. Show the setup for your calculations.

rubricPoints.criterion: Presents a definite integral with an integrand that is a product of two nonconstant factors, one of which is \( x \) and the other \( g(x) - f(x) \) (or \( f(x) - g(x) \)), e.g. \( x(g(x) - f(x)) \).
commonErrors: writes \( x^2(g(x) - f(x)) \) (squares the height)
writes \( (g(x) - f(x)) \) alone with no height factor x
uses limits other than 0 to 3

rubricPoints.criterion: Evaluates to 7.704930 and reports the volume as 7.705 (or 7.704), accurate to three places after the decimal point.
commonErrors: reports the area 5.137 instead of the volume
reports -7.705 with no sign resolution
computes the antiderivative incorrectly (missing the \( x \) factor in integration by parts)

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Write, but do not evaluate, an integral expression for the volume of the solid generated when the region R is rotated about the horizontal line \( y = -2 \).

rubricPoints.criterion: Presents a definite integral with an integrand of the form \( R^2 - r^2 \), where one of \( R \) or \( r \) is a correct difference \( g(x) + 2 \) (or \( f(x) + 2 \)) and the other is correct or a difference of f or g from a nonzero constant. (A response without the constant \( \pi \) remains eligible for this point and the next.)
commonErrors: writes a single square \( (g(x) + 2)^2 \) with no subtraction
writes \( R^2 + r^2 \) (sum instead of difference)
uses the shell method radius form instead of an annulus

rubricPoints.criterion: Writes the correct integrand \( (g(x) + 2)^2 - (f(x) + 2)^2 \) (or \( (f(x) + 2)^2 - (g(x) + 2)^2 \) when the reversal is resolved by the sign, limits, or both), with the factor \( \pi \), or a mathematically equivalent expression.
commonErrors: writes \( (g(x) - 2)^2 \) with the wrong constant sign
omits the constant 2 shift entirely, using \( f(x)^2 - g(x)^2 \)
reverses the difference of squares with no resolution
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: \pi\int_0^3 ((g(x) + 2)^2 - (f(x) + 2)^2)\,dx where R = g + 2 and r = f + 2

rubricPoints.criterion: Includes all three of the limits \( x = 0 \) to \( x = 3 \), the constant \( \pi \), and the differential dx in the final integral. (A response with a reversed difference of squares must resolve it with the constant or limits AND include dx to earn this point.)
commonErrors: omits the factor \( \pi \)
omits the differential dx
uses limits 0 to 2 (or another wrong interval)
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: \pi\int_0^3 ((g(x) + 2)^2 - (f(x) + 2)^2)\,dx with all of \pi, 0 to 3, and dx

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: It can be shown that \( g'(x) = 1 + \pi\cos(\pi x) \). Find the value of \( x \), for \( 0 < x < 1 \), at which the line tangent to the graph of f is parallel to the line tangent to the graph of g.

rubricPoints.criterion: Sets \( f'(x) = g'(x) \), giving \( 2x - 2 = 1 + \pi\cos(\pi x) \), or a general statement such as \( f'(x) = g'(x) \) with correct substitution of either derivative.
commonErrors: uses \( f(x) = g(x) \) instead of the derivatives
computes \( f'(x) = 2x^2 - 2x \) or another incorrect derivative
writes \( 2x - 2 = 1 + \sin(\pi x) \) (drops the factor \( \pi \) on the cosine)
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: f'(x) = 2x - 2 and g'(x) = 1 + \pi\cos(\pi x), so 2x - 2 = 1 + \pi\cos(\pi x)
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: f(x) = g(x) solved instead of f'(x) = g'(x)

rubricPoints.criterion: Reports \( x = 0.675819 \), so \( x = 0.676 \) (or 0.675), accurate to three places after the decimal point.
commonErrors: reports the value 0.675819 with no solution work
reports where the curves intersect (around 0.4) instead of where the tangents are parallel
reports the value to only two places
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Solving 2x - 2 = 1 + \pi\cos(\pi x) numerically gives x = 0.675819, so x = 0.676
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: x = 0.676 unsupported or x = 0.4 (an intersection of the graphs)

sampleResponse: (a) Area = \( \int_0^3 (g(x) - f(x))\,dx = \int_0^3 (x + \sin(\pi x) - x^2 + 2x)\,dx = 5.136620 \), so the area of R is 5.137. (b) Volume = \( \int_0^3 x(g(x) - f(x))\,dx = 7.704930 \), so the volume is 7.705. (c) Rotating about \( y = -2 \), Volume = \( \pi\int_0^3 \left((g(x) + 2)^2 - (f(x) + 2)^2\right)\,dx \). (d) \( f'(x) = 2x - 2 \) and \( g'(x) = 1 + \pi\cos(\pi x) \); the tangents are parallel when \( 2x - 2 = 1 + \pi\cos(\pi x) \), giving \( x = 0.675819 \), so \( x = 0.676 \).

title: Reading Rates
topic: Trapezoidal Approximation, IVT, and Polynomial Integration
prompt:

parts.text: Approximate \( R'(1) \) using the average rate of change of R over the interval \( 0 \le t \le 2 \). Show the work that leads to your answer. Indicate units of measure.

computes \( \frac{90 - 100}{2} = -5 \) with the wrong sign
uses a different interval such as \( 0 \) to \( 8 \)

rubricPoints.criterion: Indicates the units words per minute per minute (equivalently words per min^2), whether or not they are attached to the value.
commonErrors: gives units of 'words per minute' (missing the second per-minute)
gives units of 'words'
no units at all

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Must there be a value \( c \), for \( 0 < c < 10 \), such that \( R(c) = 155 \)? Justify your answer.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Use a trapezoidal sum with the three subintervals indicated by the data in the table to approximate the value of \( \int_0^{10} R(t)\,dt \). Show the work that leads to your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: Presents the form of a trapezoidal sum with three terms, each a product of a midpoint height and a width, e.g. \( \frac{R(0)+R(2)}{2}(2-0) + \frac{R(2)+R(8)}{2}(8-2) + \frac{R(8)+R(10)}{2}(10-8) \), with at least five of the six factors correct.
commonErrors: uses 0, 2, 8, 10 with an incorrect width (e.g. 5 for the middle subinterval)

rubricPoints.criterion: Computes \( \frac{190}{2}(2) + \frac{250}{2}(6) + \frac{312}{2}(2) = 190 + 750 + 312 = 1252 \), with the answer supported by the work.
commonErrors: arithmetic error in 190 + 750 + 312
reports 1252 with no trapezoidal-sum work shown

rubricPoints.exampleFailing: 2504 (no division by 2) reported as the trapezoidal sum

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: A teacher also starts reading at time \( t = 0 \) minutes and continues reading for the next 10 minutes. The rate at which the teacher reads is modeled by the function W defined by \( W(t) = -\frac{3}{10}t^2 + 8t + 100 \), where \( W(t) \) is measured in words per minute. Based on the model, how many words has the teacher read by the end of the 10 minutes? Show the work that leads to your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: Presents the definite (or indefinite) integral \( \int_0^{10} W(t)\,dt = \int_0^{10}\left(-\frac{3}{10}t^2 + 8t + 100\right)\,dt \), with or without the differential dt.
commonErrors: uses limits 0 to 10 but integrates a different function (e.g. R(t) values)
writes only W(10) - W(0)
omits the integral entirely
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: W(10) = 150 evaluated as if it were the total words

rubricPoints.criterion: Computes the correct antiderivative \( -\frac{1}{10}t^3 + 4t^2 + 100t \), with or without the constant of integration.
commonErrors: computes \( -\frac{3}{10}\frac{t^3}{3} = -\frac{3}{30}t^3 \) incorrectly
forgets to multiply \( 8t \) by \( \frac{1}{2} \) (writes \( 8t^2 \))
writes \( -\frac{1}{10}t^3 + 4t^2 \) but drops the 100t term
evaluates the antiderivative at the wrong endpoint
computes -100 + 400 + 1000 with an arithmetic error
reports 1300 as the rate, not the total
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: 1300 with no work or a wrong antiderivative evaluation

sampleResponse: (a) \( R'(1) \approx \frac{R(2)-R(0)}{2-0} = \frac{100-90}{2} = 5 \) words per minute per minute. (b) \( R(0) = 90 < 155 \) and \( R(10) = 162 > 155 \); R is differentiable, hence continuous, so by the Intermediate Value Theorem there is a c in (0,10) with \( R(c) = 155 \). (c) \( \int_0^{10} R(t)\,dt \approx (2)\frac{90+100}{2} + (6)\frac{100+150}{2} + (2)\frac{150+162}{2} = 190 + 750 + 312 = 1252 \). (d) \( \int_0^{10} W(t)\,dt = \left[-\frac{1}{10}t^3 + 4t^2 + 100t\right]_0^{10} = -100 + 400 + 1000 = 1300 \) words.

title: Accumulation Function from a Graph
topic: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus and Graph Analysis

stimulus.content: The figure shows the graph of f on [-6, 12]: a lower semicircle of radius 3 on [-6, 0], an upper semicircle of radius 3 on [0, 6], and the line segment from (6, 0) to (12, 3). (The figure is not embedded in this data file.)

prompt: The continuous function f is defined on the closed interval \( -6 \le x \le 12 \). The graph of f, consisting of two semicircles and one line segment, is shown in the figure. Let g be the function defined by \( g(x) = \int_{-6}^{x} f(t)\,dt \).

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Find \( g'(8) \). Give a reason for your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: States \( g'(x) = f(x) \), \( g'(8) = f(8) \), or otherwise applies the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus in part (a).
commonErrors: states \( g'(8) = f(8) - f(6) \) (misapplies the FTC)
gives only f(8) with no statement tying it to g'
computes g(8) - g(6) instead of the derivative
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, g'(x) = f(x)

rubricPoints.criterion: Reports \( g'(8) = f(8) = 1 \), read from the line segment of the graph (the segment from (6, 0) to (12, 3) has f(8) = 1).
commonErrors: reads f(8) = 0 or f(8) = 2
reports the area \( \int_0^8 f \) instead of the value of f
computes the slope of the segment at the wrong point

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Find all values of x in the open interval \( -6 < x < 12 \) at which the graph of g has a point of inflection. Give a reason for your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: States the points of inflection: \( x = -3 \), \( x = 3 \), and \( x = 6 \), with no other/additional values in the open interval declared to be points of inflection.
commonErrors: includes x = 0 as a point of inflection
declares additional x-values beyond -3, 3, and 6
gives only two of the three values

rubricPoints.criterion: Gives a reason tied to the graph of f: g has a point of inflection where f changes from increasing to decreasing or from decreasing to increasing (where f attains a relative extremum).
commonErrors: says 'g changes concavity there' without reference to f
says g'' = f' changes sign there without reference to the given graph of f
uses an ambiguous term such as 'the function' or 'the graph'
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: because f changes from decreasing to increasing at x = -3 and x = 6, and from increasing to decreasing at x = 3
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: 'g changes concavity there' with no tie to f

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Find \( g(12) \) and \( g(0) \). Label your answers.

rubricPoints.criterion: Reports \( g(12) = 9 \), with or without supporting work, and labels the answer as g(12). Unlabeled values do not earn the point.
commonErrors: gives 9 without the label g(12)
computes \( \int_{-6}^{12} f \) as 0 (forgetting the triangle)
reports g(12) = -9

rubricPoints.criterion: Reports \( g(0) = -\frac{9\pi}{2} \), with or without supporting work, and labels the answer as g(0). Unlabeled values do not earn the point.
commonErrors: gives \( \frac{9\pi}{2} \) (wrong sign, treats the semicircle area as positive)
gives 0 for g(0)
reports \( \frac{9\pi}{2} \) without the label g(0)

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Find the value of x at which g attains an absolute minimum on the closed interval \( -6 \le x \le 12 \). Justify your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: Considers \( g'(x) = f(x) = 0 \) (candidates x = 0 and x = 6) or \( g'(x) = 0 \), or discusses the sign of \( g'(x) \) / critical points of g.
commonErrors: just presents x = 0 and x = 6 with no equation
considers \( g(x) = 0 \) instead of \( g'(x) = 0 \)
omits the endpoints from the candidate list
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: g'(x) = f(x) = 0, so x = 0 and x = 6 are candidates

rubricPoints.criterion: Makes a global argument: compares \( g(-6) = 0 \), \( g(0) = -\frac{9\pi}{2} \), \( g(6) = 0 \), and \( g(12) = 9 \) (and no other x-values), or shows \( f(x) \le 0 \) for \( -6 \le x < 0 \) and \( f(x) \ge 0 \) for \( 0 < x \le 12 \).
commonErrors: uses a First or Second Derivative Test only (a local argument)
omits one of the candidate evaluations
compares values outside the interval
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: The smallest of g(-6) = 0, g(0) = -9\pi/2, g(6) = 0, and g(12) = 9 is g(0)
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: sign-change of g' alone with no global comparison

rubricPoints.criterion: Reports \( x = 0 \).
commonErrors: reports x = 6
reports the minimum value \( -\frac{9\pi}{2} \) instead of the x-value
reports x = 12
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Therefore g attains its absolute minimum at x = 0

sampleResponse: (a) By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, \( g'(x) = f(x) \), so \( g'(8) = f(8) = 1 \). (b) The graph of g has a point of inflection where f changes from increasing to decreasing or from decreasing to increasing, i.e. at \( x = -3 \), \( x = 3 \), and \( x = 6 \). (c) \( g(12) = \int_{-6}^{12} f(t)\,dt = \frac{1}{2}(6)(3) = 9 \), and \( g(0) = \int_{-6}^{0} f(t)\,dt = -\frac{1}{2}\pi(3)^2 = -\frac{9\pi}{2} \). (d) \( g'(x) = f(x) = 0 \) at \( x = 0 \) and \( x = 6 \). Comparing \( g(-6) = 0 \), \( g(0) = -9\pi/2 \), \( g(6) = 0 \), and \( g(12) = 9 \), the absolute minimum occurs at \( x = 0 \).

title: Two Particles on the x-axis
prompt: Two particles, H and J, are moving along the x-axis. For \( 0 \le t \le 5 \), the position of particle H at time t is given by \( x_H(t) = e^{t^2 - 4t} \), and the velocity of particle J at time t is given by \( v_J(t) = 2t(t^2 - 1)^3 \).

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Find the velocity of particle H at time \( t = 1 \). Show the work that leads to your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: Differentiates: \( x_H'(t) = v_H(t) = (2t - 4)e^{t^2 - 4t} \), or an equivalent form such as \( (2\cdot 1 - 4)e^{1 - 4} \).
commonErrors: uses \( v_H(t) = e^{t^2-4t} \) without differentiating
applies the chain rule incorrectly (writes \( e^{t^2-4t} \) with only a factor of 2t)
confuses particle H's value with particle J's velocity
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: e^{t^2-4t} reported as the velocity with no derivative

rubricPoints.criterion: Reports \( v_H(1) = -2e^{-3} \), with supporting work.
commonErrors: reports \( 2e^{-3} \) (wrong sign)
reports \( -2e \) (evaluates the exponent as 1 instead of -3)
reports \( -2 \) (drops the exponential factor)

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: During what open intervals of time t, for \( 0 < t < 5 \), are particles H and J moving in opposite directions? Give a reason for your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: Considers the sign of a velocity: sets \( x_H'(t) = 0 \), \( v_H(t) = 0 \), or \( v_J(t) = 0 \) (or identifies \( t = 2 \) for H and \( t = 1 \) for J with no other zeros in \( 0 < t < 5 \), or identifies the interval \( 1 < t < 2 \)).
commonErrors: never sets any velocity to zero to find the sign-change times
finds only one of the two sign-change times
uses t = 0 and t = 5 as the sign-change times
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: never considers where either velocity is zero

rubricPoints.criterion: Provides a correct analysis of the sign of velocity or direction of motion on \( 0 < t < 5 \) for particle H or for particle J.
commonErrors: states signs on the wrong intervals
gives only the roots with no sign analysis
analyzes only values outside the interval
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: v_H(t) < 0 for 0 < t < 2 and v_H(t) > 0 for 2 < t < 5 (H moves left then right)
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: says H 'changes direction' without sign analysis

rubricPoints.criterion: Provides correct sign/direction analyses for both particles and concludes that they move in opposite directions on \( 1 < t < 2 \).
commonErrors: has a sign error in one particle's analysis
concludes the wrong interval (e.g. 0 < t < 1 or 2 < t < 5)
gives both analyses but never states the interval
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: J moves left for 0 < t < 1 and right for 1 < t < 5; H moves left for 0 < t < 2 and right for 2 < t < 5, so only for 1 < t < 2 do they move in opposite directions

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: It can be shown that \( v_J'(2) > 0 \). Is the speed of particle J increasing, decreasing, or neither at time \( t = 2 \)? Give a reason for your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: States that \( v_J(2) > 0 \) (imported from part (b) or restarted) and \( v_J'(2) > 0 \) have the same sign, so the speed of particle J is increasing at \( t = 2 \).
commonErrors: concludes the speed is decreasing (signs have opposite effects for speed)
compares the magnitudes of v(2) and v'(2) instead of their signs
gives no reason for the verdict
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Because v_J(2) > 0 and v_J'(2) > 0 have the same sign, the speed is increasing

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Particle J is at position \( x = 7 \) at time \( t = 0 \). Find the position of particle J at time \( t = 2 \). Show the work that leads to your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: Writes the definite integral \( x_J(2) = 7 + \int_0^2 v_J(t)\,dt = 7 + \int_0^2 2t(t^2 - 1)^3\,dt \) (or an indefinite integral with integrand \( v_J(t) \)).
commonErrors: writes \( \int_0^2 v_J(t)\,dt \) but forgets the initial position 7
uses the wrong integrand (e.g. \( 2t(t^2 - 1)^2 \))
integrates from 0 to 5 instead of 0 to 2

rubricPoints.criterion: Computes the antiderivative \( \frac{1}{4}(t^2 - 1)^4 \) (the form \( k(t^2 - 1)^4 \) with \( k > 0 \)), with or without the constant of integration.
commonErrors: writes \( (t^2 - 1)^4 \) with no \( \frac{1}{4} \) factor
writes \( \frac{1}{8}(t^2 - 1)^4 \) (wrong constant from u-substitution)
writes \( \frac{1}{4}(t^2 - 1)^3 \) (wrong exponent)

rubricPoints.criterion: Evaluates to \( 7 + \frac{1}{4}(3^4 - (-1)^4) = 7 + \frac{1}{4}(80) = 27 \), reporting the position 27.
commonErrors: evaluates \( (2^2 - 1)^4 = 81 \) but uses the wrong lower limit
computes \( 7 + 20 = 27 \) but loses the +7 somewhere
reports the displacement 20 instead of the position 27

sampleResponse: (a) \( v_H(t) = x_H'(t) = (2t - 4)e^{t^2 - 4t} \), so \( v_H(1) = -2e^{-3} \). (b) \( v_H(t) = 0 \) at \( t = 2 \): \( v_H < 0 \) for \( 0 < t < 2 \) and \( v_H > 0 \) for \( 2 < t < 5 \). \( v_J(t) = 0 \) at \( t = 1 \): \( v_J < 0 \) for \( 0 < t < 1 \) and \( v_J > 0 \) for \( 1 < t < 5 \). So the particles move in opposite directions on \( 1 < t < 2 \). (c) \( v_J(2) = 108 > 0 \) and \( v_J'(2) = 486 > 0 \) have the same sign, so the speed of particle J is increasing at \( t = 2 \). (d) \( x_J(2) = 7 + \int_0^2 2t(t^2 - 1)^3\,dt = 7 + \left[\frac{1}{4}(t^2 - 1)^4\right]_0^2 = 7 + \frac{1}{4}(3^4 - (-1)^4) = 7 + 20 = 27 \).

title: Implicit Curve and a Moving Particle
prompt: Consider the curve G defined by the equation \( y^3 - y^2 - y + \frac{1}{4}x^2 = 0 \).

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Show that \( \frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{x}{2(3y^2 - 2y - 1)} \).

rubricPoints.criterion: Performs the correct implicit differentiation of \( y^3 - y^2 - y + \frac{1}{4}x^2 = 0 \), e.g. \( (3y^2 - 2y - 1)\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{x}{2} \).
commonErrors: differentiates \( \frac{1}{4}x^2 \) as \( \frac{1}{4} \) instead of \( \frac{x}{2} \)
writes \( 3y^2\frac{dy}{dx} - 2y - 1 \) (forgets to tag the other y-terms with \( \frac{dy}{dx} \))
differentiates the constant 0 side incorrectly

rubricPoints.criterion: Solves the differentiated equation to exactly the given form \( \frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{x}{2(3y^2 - 2y - 1)} \), with no subsequent errors.
commonErrors: obtains \( \frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{x}{3y^2 - 2y - 1} \) (missing the factor 2)
writes \( \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{x}{2(3y^2 - 2y - 1)} \) (sign error)
makes an algebraic error while solving

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: There is a point P on the curve G near \( (2, -1) \) with x-coordinate 1.6. Use the line tangent to the curve at \( (2, -1) \) to approximate the y-coordinate of point P.

rubricPoints.criterion: Evaluates the slope of the tangent line: \( \frac{dy}{dx}\bigg|_{(2,-1)} = -\frac{2}{2(3 + 2 - 1)} = -\frac{1}{4} \), or presents the linear approximation using a slope of \( -\frac{1}{4} \).
commonErrors: computes the slope as \( -\frac{1}{3} \) or another value not equal to \( -\frac{1}{4} \)
evaluates the denominator as \( 3 - 2 + 1 = 2 \) (sign errors in \(-1\))
never evaluates the slope numerically

rubricPoints.criterion: Approximates \( y \approx -1 + \left(-\frac{1}{4}\right)(1.6 - 2) = -1 + 0.1 = -0.9 \), clearly using the tangent line at \( x = 1.6 \).
commonErrors: uses the slope \( -\frac{1}{4} \) but computes \( -1 - \frac{1}{4}(1.6 - 2) \) incorrectly
uses a slope other than \( -\frac{1}{4} \) that was not declared as the value of the derivative
reports the value of y at x = 1.6 without showing the tangent line use

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: For \( x > 0 \) and \( y > 0 \), there is a point S on the curve G at which the line tangent to the curve at that point is vertical. Find the y-coordinate of point S. Show the work that leads to your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: Sets the denominator of \( \frac{dy}{dx} \) equal to 0: \( 2(3y^2 - 2y - 1) = 0 \), \( 3y^2 - 2y - 1 = 0 \), or the factored form \( (3y + 1)(y - 1) = 0 \).
commonErrors: sets the numerator of \( \frac{dy}{dx} \) equal to 0 instead
sets \( \frac{dy}{dx} \) equal to 0 rather than undefined
never sets anything equal to 0 and jumps to the answer

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies \( y = 1 \) as the y-coordinate (the solution with \( y > 0 \); \( y = -\frac{1}{3} \) is rejected).
commonErrors: reports both \( y = 1 \) and \( y = -\frac{1}{3} \) without rejecting the negative one
reports \( y = -\frac{1}{3} \)
reports the x-coordinate of S instead
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Because y > 0, the only solution is y = 1
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: y = -1/3 also included as an answer

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: A particle moves along the curve H defined by the equation \( 2xy + \ln y = 8 \). At the instant when the particle is at the point \( (4, 1) \), \( \frac{dx}{dt} = 3 \). Find \( \frac{dy}{dt} \) at that instant. Show the work that leads to your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: Implicitly differentiates \( 2xy + \ln y = 8 \) with respect to t (product rule on \( 2xy \), derivative of \( \ln y \) carrying \( \frac{dy}{dt} \), right side 0), with at most one error.
commonErrors: differentiates \( 2xy \) as \( 2\frac{dy}{dt} \) (misses the product rule) or as \( 2y\frac{dx}{dt} \) alone
writes \( \frac{d}{dt}\ln y = \frac{1}{y} \) without the \( \frac{dy}{dt} \) factor
differentiates with respect to x instead of t

rubricPoints.criterion: Obtains the correct differentiated equation \( 2y\frac{dx}{dt} + \left(2x + \frac{1}{y}\right)\frac{dy}{dt} = 0 \), or equivalently each of the terms \( 2y\frac{dx}{dt} \), \( 2x\frac{dy}{dt} \), and \( \frac{1}{y}\frac{dy}{dt} \).
commonErrors: has a sign error in one of the terms
writes \( 2xy \) differentiated as \( 2y\frac{dx}{dt} + 2x \) with no \( \frac{dy}{dt} \)
drops the \( \frac{1}{y}\frac{dy}{dt} \) term

rubricPoints.criterion: Substitutes \( (x, y) = (4, 1) \) and \( \frac{dx}{dt} = 3 \): \( 2(1)(3) + \left(2(4) + 1\right)\frac{dy}{dt} = 0 \), so \( 6 + 9\frac{dy}{dt} = 0 \) and \( \frac{dy}{dt} = -\frac{2}{3} \).
commonErrors: substitutes \( x = 4 \) and \( y = 1 \) in the wrong spots
computes \( 2(4) + \frac{1}{1} = 9 \) but then solves \( 6 + 9\frac{dy}{dt} = 0 \) incorrectly
reports \( \frac{dy}{dt} = \frac{2}{3} \) (sign error)

sampleResponse: (a) Differentiating \( y^3 - y^2 - y + \frac{1}{4}x^2 = 0 \): \( (3y^2 - 2y - 1)\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{x}{2} \), so \( \frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{x}{2(3y^2 - 2y - 1)} \). (b) At \( (2, -1) \), \( \frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{2}{2(3 + 2 - 1)} = -\frac{1}{4} \), so \( y \approx -1 - \frac{1}{4}(1.6 - 2) = -0.9 \). (c) The tangent is vertical when \( 3y^2 - 2y - 1 = 0 \), i.e. \( (3y + 1)(y - 1) = 0 \). With \( y > 0 \), the y-coordinate is \( y = 1 \). (d) Differentiating \( 2xy + \ln y = 8 \) with respect to t: \( 2y\frac{dx}{dt} + 2x\frac{dy}{dt} + \frac{1}{y}\frac{dy}{dt} = 0 \). At \( (4, 1) \) with \( \frac{dx}{dt} = 3 \): \( 6 + 9\frac{dy}{dt} = 0 \), so \( \frac{dy}{dt} = -\frac{2}{3} \).
